title: BREAKING — Beyond the 956: Super Typhoon Champi's 10-Mile Near Miss on Guam — Island Recovering as Storm Threatens Okinawa and a New Disturbance Forms
excerpt: Super Typhoon Champi passed about 10 miles south of Guam on October 18, knocking out power to half the island under a presidential emergency declaration. Guam's power is now 99% restored, no warnings are in effect, and Champi — still a typhoon at 92 mph — is threatening Okinawa while forecasters watch new disturbance Invest 97W in the Marshall Islands.
content:
🌎 BEYOND THE 956

BREAKING UPDATE — Friday, October 23, 2026 (Saturday, October 24 in Guam)

Guam is recovering after Super Typhoon Champi passed about 10 miles south of the island's southern tip in the early hours of Sunday, October 18 — and the storm, still a typhoon, is now threatening Japan's Okinawa islands this weekend, while forecasters watch a new tropical disturbance forming in the Marshall Islands.

The near miss. Champi made its closest point of approach to Guam at 4:26 a.m. Chamorro Standard Time on October 18, passing roughly 10 miles (16 km) south of Merizo, according to The Watchers, citing Joint Typhoon Warning Center post-analysis. The storm was upgraded to a super typhoon about three hours after it passed the island. Champi later reached maximum sustained winds of 185 mph, tying Super Typhoon Sinlaku as the strongest tropical cyclone on Earth so far in 2026 by wind speed, according to Associated Press reporting.

The emergency. Before the storm arrived, Governor Lou Leon Guerrero declared a state of emergency and placed Guam in Condition of Readiness 1 (COR 1), its highest alert level, effective 1 p.m. on October 17, according to Guam Homeland Security and the Office of Civil Defense (GHS/OCD). President Donald Trump approved presidential emergency declarations for both Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, authorizing the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to coordinate federal assistance, according to the White House. The National Weather Service in Tiyan had a Typhoon Warning in effect for Guam and Rota, with tropical storm warnings and a typhoon watch for Tinian and Saipan, and forecast 6 to 12 inches of rain, dangerous surf of 15 to 20 feet, and coastal flooding of up to 7 feet in southern Guam. Five Guam Department of Education emergency shelters opened with a combined capacity of 1,964 people, and Astumbo Elementary School reached full occupancy before the eyewall passed, according to the GHS/OCD Joint Information Center. The U.S. Coast Guard set Port Condition ZULU across Guam, Saipan, Tinian and Rota, halting port operations.

The impacts. By 7:50 a.m. on October 18, about half of Guam had lost power as additional feeders tripped offline, according to the Guam Power Authority (GPA) in updates relayed by the Joint Information Center — although Guam Memorial Hospital, Naval Base Guam, Andersen Air Force Base and the Tumon hotel district stayed online. The Ugum Surface Water Treatment Plant shut down because of storm-driven turbidity, affecting water service in southern villages, officials said. Guam Memorial Hospital reported three storm-related visits, including one minor injury. Governor Leon Guerrero later said damage on the island was minimal compared with the devastating direct hit forecasters had feared. Public and Catholic schools were closed Monday, October 19, for damage assessments.

The recovery. The last tropical cyclone warnings for Guam ended Sunday evening, October 18, and the island returned to COR 4, its normal readiness level. By Monday morning, GPA reported 90 percent of transmission lines restored, all 30 critical substations energized, and 47 of 67 distribution feeders energized or partially energized, while about 653 water accounts — roughly 1.5 percent of customers — were without service. By Wednesday, October 21, GPA reported the islandwide power system was 99 percent recovered.

Where Champi is now. Champi is no longer a threat to Guam. Japan Meteorological Agency data on Friday, October 23 (03:00 UTC) still listed Champi as a typhoon with 92 mph winds, with Okinawa's Sakishima Islands in its path on October 24 and Kyushu around October 26. In Taiwan, one person died after being swept away by waves on Liuqiu island on October 22 and 94 people were injured, according to Associated Press reporting via ABC News on October 23. Champi will not reach the U.S. mainland.

Guam today — and the next system to watch. The National Weather Service Guam reported Friday night local time that there are no active tropical cyclones and no watches, warnings or advisories in effect for Guam or the Marianas. Guam's Saturday, October 24 forecast calls for mostly cloudy skies and scattered showers, and the NWS coastal waters forecast notes a broad trough extending from tropical disturbance 98W in eastern Yap State bringing patchy showers and seas of 6 to 8 feet. Separately, the NWS Tropical Weather Discussion issued at 12:54 p.m. ChST on Friday, October 23 says a new disturbance, Invest 97W, is centered over the northern Marshall Islands near 12°N, 166°E and is the subject of a Joint Typhoon Warning Center Tropical Cyclone Formation Alert rated "high," meaning development into a tropical depression is expected within 24 hours. Forecasters expect 97W to stay near the Marshalls through Saturday, then lift north late Saturday night, likely as a tropical depression or low-end tropical storm. It is not currently forecast to threaten Guam, but Webb Watch 956 will keep tracking it.

Update — October 23, 2026 (evening)

Champi's toll has reached land beyond Guam. Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday, killing one person — a man swept away by waves off the island of Liuqiu — and injuring more than 500, according to Taiwan's fire department, Reuters reported. Coastal gusts reached about 227 kph (141 mph); Taipower said more than 288,000 homes lost electricity at one point, and the transport ministry cancelled 242 flights Saturday after nearly 1,000 on Friday. The storm, weakening after its earlier super-typhoon peak, is tracking north toward the Chinese coast and eventually southern Japan, per Taiwan's Central Weather Administration. Webb Watch 956 will continue to track the storm's impacts.

Update — October 24, 2026

Typhoon Champi is bearing down on Japan's Okinawa and Sakishima Islands. Japan Airlines, All Nippon Airways, and Skymark canceled more than 100 flights between Thursday and Sunday — JAL announced 120 cancellations on October 22–23 and ANA 55 over the same two days — affecting more than 11,000 passengers, with ANA canceling all its Miyako and Ishigaki flights on October 23. Nearly 8,400 households lost power in Okinawa, the BBC reported, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged residents to remain vigilant against storm-force winds, landslides, and storm surges. The storm, weakening after its super-typhoon peak, is forecast to approach Kyushu on Monday before becoming an extratropical cyclone by Tuesday. No new watches or warnings are in effect for Guam.

Update — October 24, 2026 (Saturday morning, Japan time)

Champi has moved past Japan's Sakishima Islands and into the East China Sea. The Japan Meteorological Agency placed the storm at 9 a.m. Saturday about 50 kilometers north-northeast of Yonaguni Island, with a central pressure of 980 hectopascals, sustained winds of 108 kph and gusts up to 162 kph, according to JMA reporting summarized Saturday. Ishigaki Island recorded a maximum gust of 126 kph shortly after 9:20 a.m. The storm, weakened from its super-typhoon peak to tropical-storm strength, is forecast to move north through Sunday, approach the Kyushu region on Monday morning and become an extratropical cyclone by Tuesday. The agency urged caution for heavy rain in northern Kyushu, the Chugoku and Kinki regions and the Hokuriku region through around Monday. No new watches or warnings are in effect for Guam.

Update — October 24, 2026 (Saturday, Japan time)

Champi's passage over the Sakishima Islands brought the storm's hardest recorded punch in Japan so far. As it crossed the islands on Friday night, the Japan Meteorological Agency briefly upgraded it back to a "very strong" typhoon, with sustained winds of 45 meters per second and gusts up to 60 meters per second (134 mph) near Yonaguni. Iriomote Island recorded a record October gust of 51.7 meters per second (116 mph), and Hateruma and Yonaguni also set October records. About 14,470 households lost power, most of them on Ishigaki and in Taketomi, and Miyako Airport measured 336 millimeters of rain in 24 hours. Okinawa officials reported two storm-related injuries, and travelers waited on Ishigaki for flights to resume. Taiwan's fire department refined its toll to 527 injured, with the death toll holding at one. The storm, now in the East China Sea, is tracking toward the Chinese coast — where authorities evacuated tens of thousands of people in Shanghai and suspended some train services — before its expected approach to Kyushu on Monday. No new watches or warnings are in effect for Guam.

Update — October 24, 2026 (Saturday afternoon, Japan time)

Champi, now weakened to a tropical storm, continued north over the East China Sea on Saturday afternoon. The Japan Meteorological Agency placed the storm at 3 p.m. about 250 kilometers north of Yonaguni Island, moving north-northeast at 20 kph with a central pressure of 985 hectopascals and sustained winds of 108 kph. Iriomote Island recorded 567 millimeters of rain in 48 hours through early Saturday afternoon, a record for the location, according to JMA reporting. Okinawa Electric Power said about 12,830 customers were still without electricity as of 5 p.m. Saturday, and the storm was packing gusts of around 150 kph even as it weakened. Forecasters now expect the weakening system to become extratropical by Tuesday, and some guidance has it dissipating before reaching Kyushu; other guidance still takes it over central to northern Kyushu on Monday. Unlike earlier expectations of a China-coast approach, the storm is now not expected to make landfall on the Chinese coast. No new watches or warnings are in effect for Guam.

Update — October 25, 2026 (Sunday, Japan time)

Champi kept weakening over the East China Sea on Sunday as it began its transition into an extratropical cyclone. The Joint Typhoon Warning Center placed the tropical storm about 659 kilometers southwest of Sasebo, Japan, tracking northeast at 20 kph, and said the transition could be complete within 24 hours — or the storm could weaken into a trough and dissipate before completing it. The Japan Meteorological Agency said Champi could still approach Kyushu on Monday before turning extratropical and moving toward waters off western Shikoku, urging caution over heavy rain from a lingering weather front across eastern and western Japan. South Korea felt the storm first: the Korea Meteorological Administration raised a typhoon warning for waters far south of Jeju at 4 a.m. Sunday, with 120 millimeters or more of additional rain expected through Monday and a closest pass about 220 kilometers southeast of Seogwipo around 3 a.m. Monday. Jeju has already endured three days of heavy rain that grounded flights, halted ferries and closed trails on Mount Halla, where Samgak Peak recorded 285 millimeters of accumulated rain as of 8:30 a.m. Sunday. No new watches or warnings are in effect for Guam.

Update — October 26, 2026 (Monday, Japan time)

Champi's run as a tropical system is over. The Joint Typhoon Warning Center issued its final warning at 6 p.m. UTC on Sunday, October 25, placing the system about 302 kilometers southwest of Sasebo, Japan, with sustained winds of 65 kilometers per hour and a central pressure of 1,002 hectopascals. Satellite data showed the system had opened into a trough, with storm-force winds confined to its northeastern side, and forecasters said it would keep degrading as it tracked northeast, with elevated winds possible as the trough passed over Kyushu.

The heavy rain did not end with the tropical system. Reporting from Tokyo on Monday said Champi had weakened into an extratropical cyclone overnight, while its humid air continued to feed a front stalled over the Japanese archipelago, with heavy rain forecast through Tuesday, October 27 — up to 200 millimeters in northern Kyushu and Shikoku and 150 millimeters in southern Kyushu, plus heavy rain in the Kanto region including Tokyo. On Tsushima Island in Nagasaki Prefecture, 24-hour precipitation exceeded 200 millimeters, breaking the island's October record, and Japan's Meteorological Agency warned of possible landslides and flooding.

In Okinawa, where Champi had already passed, power was cut to about 13,000 households and some areas also lost water service, prompting Okinawa Prefecture to request disaster relief from the Self-Defense Forces, according to the Tokyo reporting. No new watches or warnings are in effect for Guam.
